stem: Mireille, a collegiate 400 m hurdler, tells the consultant, "One weekend I'm shaking in the call room and sure I'll hit a hurdle. The next weekend, same coach, same teammates, I walk out calm and trusting my legs." The consultant would like to set numbers for these swings beside her finishing times at each of the next six meets. Which questionnaire should the consultant give her?
options: The Sport Anxiety Scale-2 (SAS-2)
The Test of Performance Strategies (TOPS)
The Competitive State Anxiety Inventory-2 (CSAI-2)
The Profile of Mood States (POMS)
rationales: The SAS-2 describes how anxious an athlete tends to be across competitions. Mireille's report differs from one weekend to the next, and a trait score would not follow that.
The TOPS asks how often an athlete uses mental skills in practice and competition. Her swings are in how she feels, not in which skills she uses.
Best. Her shaking, doubt, and trust in her legs change from meet to meet, so a state measure with somatic, cognitive, and self-confidence scores, taken before each race, can be set beside her times.
The POMS covers broad moods such as vigor, fatigue, and anger. It has a tension score but nothing on self-confidence, half of what swings for her.
takeaway: Symptoms that change from event to event call for a state measure taken at each event.

stem: A professional rugby club's coach sent Casimir, a fly-half, to the consultant after several poor goal-kicking games. Casimir arrived guarded. Half an hour into the intake he has said that the misses are costing him sleep, that he wants to be the one who takes the late kicks again, and that a quiet spell alone on the tee after training used to settle him. "I could pick that up again Monday," he says. "I should have done it weeks ago." Which response best fits motivational interviewing?
options: "How do you see yourself getting started?"
"What bothers you most about how it's been going?"
"It was your coach's idea to come, not yours."
"Would you like to hear what has helped other kickers?"
rationales: Best. Desire, ability, need, and a date have all come from Casimir, signs that he is ready to move from evoking to planning. An open question about starting leaves the plan in his hands.
An evoking question draws out concern when a client has voiced little. Casimir has voiced plenty and has turned toward action; going back would slow him down.
Reflecting the pressure he arrived under helps while he is guarded. He has since moved well past that point.
Offering information with permission suits a client who wants change and has no idea how. Casimir has named something that worked for him.
takeaway: Listen for mobilizing change talk: when the client has a reason and a way, move to planning.

stem: The coach of a collegiate field hockey team sends Adaeze to the consultant because she "chokes" in penalty shootouts. She has converted 3 of 11 in matches. In training, against the same goalkeepers with nobody keeping score, she has converted 21 of 80. Her teammates manage more than half in both settings. Adaeze, who played defense until August, grins about the misses and says she'll get the hang of it. Her SAS-2 scores are ordinary for college athletes. Which working formulation best fits?
options: Worry that disrupts a well-practiced skill under pressure
Low confidence that has built up with repeated misses
Attention that strays to distractions when stakes rise
A shootout technique that she has yet to learn
rationales: Worry would show up as a gap between training and matches and, most likely, raised worry scores. Her rate is about one in four in both places.
Low confidence would show in how she talks about the next attempt. She shrugs the misses off and expects to improve.
Straying attention tied to the stakes would spare her training attempts. Those fail as often as her match attempts.
Best. She converts about a quarter of her attempts with or without pressure, is new to an attacking role, and is not anxious. "Choking" needs a drop from a level she has shown, and there is none.
takeaway: Choking means falling below your own level under pressure; check that the level exists first.

stem: At a national selection camp, a judo federation asks the consultant to meet each athlete. Bongani, who is fighting for one of two spots, hands back the ACSI-28 after two minutes. Scored, it gives him a mixed profile, with some subscales at the top and freedom from worry at the bottom. Looking at the sheet itself, the consultant sees that he circled "almost always" for every statement, whether it was about staying calm or about fretting over mistakes. Which reading of the form do his answers best support?
options: He is presenting himself well for the selectors
He answered with little regard to item content
His coping is strong overall, with worry as a soft spot
His answers describe the camp rather than his usual self
rationales: An athlete trying to look good would deny fretting over mistakes. Bongani endorsed the unflattering statements as strongly as the flattering ones.
Best. Agreeing as strongly with opposite statements is a careless or acquiescent response pattern. The mixed profile comes from reverse-scored items, so it says little about his coping.
This is what the scored profile appears to show. The subscale differences come from how items are keyed, since his answer never changed.
Answering about the present week would still yield answers that fit together. Saying he is almost always calm and almost always fretting does not.
takeaway: Look at the raw answers before the profile: identical answers to opposite items mean the scores cannot be read.

stem: Following the athletic department's intake policy, the consultant gives Marisela, a collegiate softball pitcher, a validated depression screen alongside performance measures. Her score falls in the range the department flags for follow-up. "That sounds right," she says. Sleep and energy have been poor since January, though she has had no thoughts of hurting herself. "We started medication last month and we're still adjusting it. I'm in there every Thursday." What should the consultant do about the score?
options: Walk her over to the counseling center's on-call staff
Give her the names of two clinicians near campus
Ask to send the result to the clinician treating her
Continue the intake and screen her again at midseason
rationales: A walk to on-call staff fits a student whose safety is in doubt. She reports no thoughts of self-harm.
New names help an athlete who has no care. Her weekly visits and recent medication show that she has it, and a second provider could split her treatment.
Best. She is in active treatment that is still being adjusted, so the useful step is to coordinate: with her consent, the result goes to the person who can act on it.
Routine rescreening fits a score in the normal range. Hers is in the flagged range and calls for follow-up now.
takeaway: A flagged screen needs clinical follow-up; if care is in place, coordinate with it, with consent.

stem: Rhys, a 20-year-old professional esports player, has filled out a performance profile listing fourteen qualities of a top player in his role, with a rating of himself on each for now and for where he wants to be. He and his coach agree that it is a fair picture. Three gaps stand out, each four points wide: aim in late rounds, shot-calling, and patience after early losses. There is time to work on one before the season. Which step would do most to turn the profile into a choice?
options: Rate how much each quality matters in his role
Have his coach rate him on the same qualities
Re-rate himself after reviewing some match film
Add qualities that he sees in players he admires
rationales: Best. The gaps are the same size and the ratings are trusted, so size cannot rank them. Weighting each gap by its importance to his role is the part of profiling that is missing.
A second rater helps when player and coach see him differently. The coach already accepts the picture.
Film can steady ratings that rest on mood or memory. Nobody doubts these ratings, and repeating them could leave the same three-way tie.
Widening the list helps when a player has named few qualities. Fourteen already cover the role, and more would add candidates.
takeaway: In profiling, a gap's priority depends on its size and on how much the quality matters.

stem: A high school volleyball coach asks the consultant why the team "comes apart" in close sets. Pressed for an example, she laughs. "Honestly? One day they're silent, another day they're all yelling. Sometimes nobody moves, sometimes two girls go for the same ball. I can't tell you what it is. I just know it when I see it." The consultant will watch Saturday's match. Which way of observing best suits this first look?
options: Count each player's calls on a prepared checklist
Time how long the team takes to regroup after errors
Compare calls for the ball in close and lopsided sets
Write running notes on what happens around lost points
rationales: A checklist gives precise counts once the behavior has been defined. The coach cannot yet say which behavior matters, so a checklist might count the wrong thing.
Timing suits a behavior known to drag on. The coach's examples vary, and slow regrouping is not among them.
Comparing conditions tests a specific idea about when a behavior changes. Here the behavior is still unknown.
Best. The problem is undefined and takes many forms, so open narrative notes on what comes before and after lost points can show what is worth defining and counting later.
takeaway: Count behaviors once you know which ones matter; until then, start with narrative observation.

stem: Esme, an 11-year-old competitive gymnast, has assented to work with the consultant, and her parents have given permission. Her coach says, "State finals, club meet, a pretend meet with six moms watching, it makes no difference. She frets for days, her tummy hurts, and then she blanks on beam." The consultant wants a questionnaire for the initial assessment. Which one best fits?
options: The Competitive State Anxiety Inventory-2 (CSAI-2)
The Sport Anxiety Scale-2 (SAS-2)
The Profile of Mood States (POMS)
The Athletic Coping Skills Inventory-28 (ACSI-28)
rationales: The CSAI-2 captures anxiety at one moment before an event and was developed with older athletes. Esme's pattern is the same at all meets.

Best. Fretting, stomach aches, and blanking at meets of all sizes point to a general tendency involving worry, somatic anxiety, and concentration disruption. The SAS-2 measures these and was developed for children as well as adults.
The POMS tracks general moods such as fatigue and vigor. It is not specific to performing and was not developed for children.
The ACSI-28 profiles coping skills such as coachability and goal setting. It touches on worry but not on stomach aches, and it was developed with older athletes.
takeaway: Anxiety that shows up at events of all sizes suggests a trait measure; for children, use one built for them.

stem: Nalani, a contemporary dancer, believes that one slip in an audition will finish her. With the consultant she has recalled four slips, her own and her friends', and three of those dancers were hired anyway. "So it's unlikely," she says. "But say it's me. They stop writing, somebody says 'thank you,' and then... I don't know. Lights out." She has stopped at this spot twice before. Which question best helps her think the feared outcome through?
options: "What goes through your mind as you walk into the studio?"
"What have you seen happen to dancers who slipped?"
"What would a slip say about you as a dancer?"
"What would you do in the weeks after a no?"
rationales: This question brings out an automatic thought that has not yet been put into words. Nalani has stated hers clearly.
Asking for evidence is a core Socratic move, and she has just done it. The evidence changed her estimate of the odds but not her dread of the outcome.
The downward arrow looks for the meaning beneath a thought. She is stuck on what happens next, and this would turn her toward judging herself.
Best. The odds have been examined; her picture of the outcome simply ends. Asking what would follow is decatastrophizing, and it lets her see whether she could cope.
takeaway: When the odds have been examined and dread remains, ask what would happen next and how the client would cope.

stem: Dmitri, a wheelchair basketball player on a national squad, shoots 78% on free throws through three quarters and 55% in the fourth. His coach, who rarely takes him off the court, says he loses focus. On the ACSI-28, Dmitri rates his concentration highly, and he describes the breath and cue word he uses on each attempt. Over two games the consultant saw the same breath, the same tempo, and the same cue late as early, and most of the late misses hit the front of the rim. What should the consultant do next?
options: Compare late shooting in games with fewer minutes
Code his free-throw routine over several more games
Ask what he is thinking on fourth-quarter attempts
Give the TAIS to see how his attention narrows
rationales: Best. The routine holds up and the misses fall short, so tiring arms are a strong rival to lost focus. Records of games in which he played less are a simple check before a mental formulation is settled.
Coding his routine would help if it seemed to break down or had gone unseen. In two games it did not change.
His account is in hand and matches what was seen. It cannot show why the shots fall short.
An attentional profile would suit signs that he is distracted or overloaded. Neither his reports nor his behavior shows any.
takeaway: Before settling on a mental explanation, test the physical one that the data suggest.

stem: Ezra, a first-year collegiate cross-country runner, says he grew up in a house where nobody hurried to speak. At intake the consultant has twice followed up after a few seconds of quiet, and each time he gave a polite one-line reply. Once, she had to search for a pen; when she looked up, he had begun a long, careful account of what his running means to his family. Now she asks what a good season would be. He looks at the floor, at ease, and says nothing. What should she do?
options: Put the question in simpler words
Tell him they can come back to it
Wait quietly until he speaks
Reflect that the question seems hard
rationales: Rewording helps a client who has not understood. Nothing suggests that, and it would be a third interruption.
Offering to return to a topic respects a client who does not want to discuss it. Ezra is at ease and has talked freely when given time.
Best. His fullest answer came when she happened to leave him time, and her quick follow-ups cut him short. His silence reads as thinking, and waiting adapts her pace to his way of talking.
Reflecting feeling helps when the client shows some. He is at ease, so this would put her discomfort with silence into his mouth.
takeaway: The meaning of silence varies; match your pace to the client's before treating it as a problem.

stem: A consultant takes over preseason testing at a professional women's basketball club, her only role there. The consent form, which the players signed after a question-and-answer session, says that ACSI-28 scores go to the general manager for use in roster decisions. The consultant has used the inventory for ten years. Reading down her report, the general manager says, "Twelfth and thirteenth are two points apart. That settles our last spot." Which concern bears most directly on this plan?
options: The players have not agreed to this use of their scores
The scores have little evidence behind them for this purpose
The consultant is also the players' confidential adviser
The consultant lacks the training to interpret the inventory
rationales: Lack of consent would be decisive if the players had been promised another use. Here the form named this one.
Best. The ACSI-28 describes coping skills; it was not validated for choosing between two players, and two points means little given measurement error. Consent does not make an invalid use valid.
Dual roles would matter if she also counseled the players. Testing is all she does for the club.
Competence would be the issue for someone new to the measure. She has used it for a decade.
takeaway: Even with consent, a score should be used only for decisions its validity evidence supports.

stem: Quillon, a collegiate archer, scores high in training and drops at tournaments. He insists that he does "the same mental stuff" everywhere. The consultant leafs through his log. The training pages are full of cue words, pictured shots, and slow breaths between ends. The tournament pages list arrows, scores, and the weather. The consultant would like a questionnaire that could test the pattern the log suggests. Which one fits best?
options: The Athletic Coping Skills Inventory-28 (ACSI-28)
The Sport Imagery Questionnaire (SIQ)
The Test of Attentional and Interpersonal Style (TAIS)
The Test of Performance Strategies (TOPS)
rationales: The ACSI-28 gives a general picture of coping skills. It does not separate training from tournaments.
The SIQ covers what imagery is used for. Imagery is one of several skills that vanish from his tournament pages.
The TAIS profiles attentional tendencies. The log shows a difference in skill use and says nothing about where his attention goes.
Best. The log suggests that he uses several skills in training and few of them at tournaments. The TOPS asks about the use of such strategies in practice and in competition separately.
takeaway: When the question is whether skills are used in practice and in competition, the TOPS scores both.

stem: A ballet company has hired the consultant to work with Zainab, a soloist, who has agreed in writing that the artistic director may share observations. The director sends a page. It dates three performances and tells what happened in each, describes the coaching she has tried, and notes that Zainab is radiant in studio runs and at matinees. It ends, "I need more presence from her by spring. Then I'll know you two have done it." Which question should the consultant ask the director first?
options: "What would you see if she had more presence?"
"When did you last notice this, and what happened?"
"What have you already tried with her?"
"When do you see her at her best?"
rationales: Best. The director's note is concrete about the past and vague about the target. "Presence" is the standard by which the work will be judged, so it needs to be described in observable terms.
Asking for specific incidents is the remedy for vague complaints. She has given three, with dates and details.
Earlier attempts are worth knowing, and the director has described them.
Exceptions and strengths help balance a list of faults. She has already named studio runs and matinees.
takeaway: Find what the stakeholder has left vague; often it is the standard by which success will be judged.

stem: Saskia, a professional golfer, is the one her playing partners ask about wind and slope. "She sees the whole hole," her caddie says. Over the ball it is another story: "I've still got the wind going, and the last putt, and my coach, and what if I push it. It all piles up and I swing in the middle of it." The consultant wants a questionnaire whose scores could show both sides of this. Which one fits best?
options: The Athletic Coping Skills Inventory-28 (ACSI-28)
The Test of Performance Strategies (TOPS)
The Test of Attentional and Interpersonal Style (TAIS)
The Sport Anxiety Scale-2 (SAS-2)
rationales: The ACSI-28 has one concentration score. It cannot show that she takes in the surroundings well and is overloaded by her own thoughts.
The TOPS asks about the use of skills such as self-talk and relaxation. Her description is of where her attention goes.
Best. She is strong at broad-external attention and is overloaded by internal thoughts. The TAIS gives separate scores for attentional strengths and for types of overload.
The SAS-2 includes concentration disruption as a part of anxiety. It has no score for her ability to read a hole.
takeaway: Match the instrument to the pattern: the TAIS separates attentional strengths from types of overload.

stem: The director of a youth soccer academy has noticed that after the same drill, run by the same coach, some 13-year-olds ask, "Did I beat him?" and others ask, "Was that quicker than last week?" Before a coach-education course begins, she would like to know how these two kinds of players are spread across her squads. Parents have given permission and players have assented. Which questionnaire should the consultant suggest?
options: The Athletic Identity Measurement Scale (AIMS)
The Task and Ego Orientation in Sport Questionnaire (TEOSQ)
The Perceived Motivational Climate in Sport Questionnaire (PMCSQ)
The Group Environment Questionnaire (GEQ)
rationales: The AIMS measures how strongly a person identifies with being an athlete. The players differ in how they judge a good performance.
Best. The drill and the coach are the same, so the difference lies in the players: some judge success by comparison and others by improvement. The TEOSQ measures these dispositions.
A climate measure asks what players think their coaches reward. The same coach and drill produce both questions here, so the director's interest is in the players.
The GEQ measures cohesion. How united the squads are is a separate matter from how players judge success.
takeaway: Goal orientation belongs to the player; motivational climate belongs to the setting.

stem: Callum, a collegiate lacrosse goalkeeper, has rated his confidence on game mornings for five weeks. The numbers run from 3 to 9. Asked about the 9s, he gives a new answer each time: his coach's nod, a sharp warm-up, his brother in the stands, the home crease. Asked about the 3s, he shrugs. Before planning any work, the consultant wants a questionnaire to find out what those numbers hang on. Which measure fits best?
options: The Sources of Sport-Confidence Questionnaire
A self-efficacy scale graded by difficulty of save
The self-confidence subscale of the CSAI-2
The Trait Sport-Confidence Inventory
rationales: Best. The level of his confidence is already recorded; what is unknown is where it comes from. This questionnaire covers sources such as preparation, social support, coach leadership, and environmental comfort.
A graded scale would show which saves he believes he can make. His ratings vary by day, and he has not tied them to kinds of shots.
This would give another reading of how confident he is before games, which his morning ratings already supply.
A trait score shows how confident he usually is in sport. It would not account for ups and downs.
takeaway: Knowing how confident an athlete is differs from knowing where the confidence comes from.

stem: Katarzyna, a soldier on an army rifle team, pictures shooting every night. The images come when she calls them, she says, in color, with the weight of the rifle and the smell of oil. Asked what she pictures, she says, "Oh, all sorts." Over a month she has mentioned the bolt and breath, a medal ceremony, a quarrel with a range officer, and walking calmly to the line. The consultant wants a questionnaire to help sort this out. Which one fits best?
options: The Movement Imagery Questionnaire-3 (MIQ-3)
The Test of Performance Strategies (TOPS)
The Test of Attentional and Interpersonal Style (TAIS)
The Sport Imagery Questionnaire (SIQ)
rationales: The MIQ-3 measures how easily a person can see and feel imagined movements. Her images already come readily and vividly.
The TOPS could show how often she uses imagery among other skills. It does not sort images by purpose.
The TAIS profiles attention. Nothing here is about what she attends to while shooting.
Best. She images often and well but with mixed content: skills, rewards, and emotions. The SIQ shows how often imagery serves each of its cognitive and motivational functions.
takeaway: The MIQ-3 asks how well a person can image; the SIQ asks what the imagery is used for.

stem: Since a run of trades, the coach and captains of a professional ice hockey club have watched the 14 forwards and the 8 defensemen drift apart: separate tables, separate cars, separate jokes. Within each bunch, spirits are high. The players are willing to fill out the GEQ if no names are attached, and they want to know, as much as the coach does, whether things are as bad as they look. Which way of giving and reporting the GEQ best serves this purpose?
options: Unmarked forms, reported as team averages
Coded forms, tracked for each player over the season
Forms marked by position, reported as group averages
Named forms, gone over with each player in private
rationales: Team averages are the usual report when a whole team's unity is in question. Here they would blend two groups that may see things differently.
Codes let each player's scores be linked over time. The question is about a divide that exists now.
Best. The concern is a split along position lines, and both groups are large enough for averages to keep individuals hidden. Marking position shows whether the groups see the team differently.
Named forms would support individual talks, but the players have agreed only to nameless ones and the concern lies between groups.
takeaway: Report group data at the level where the question lies, with groups large enough to protect individuals.

stem: In an intake session, Amadou, a collegiate wrestler, asks for help getting tougher about making weight. He weighs in tomorrow. He has eaten almost nothing for three days and ran in a sweat suit last night. He admits that he panics when he eats these days. Reaching for his bag, he grips the desk until the room stops turning; it happened on the stairs too, he says, and his heart has been skipping since lunch. What should the consultant do first?
options: Arrange a visit with a clinician who treats eating disorders
Take him to the sports medicine staff
Arrange a visit with the athletic department's dietitian
Help him plan how to tell his coach that he's moving up
rationales: His panic about eating calls for this, and it should follow. It can be set up once he has been seen for symptoms that could be dangerous today.
Best. Dizzy spells and an irregular heartbeat after fasting and dehydration may be a medical emergency. Prompt medical evaluation comes before any other help he needs.
A dietitian can help plan a safe weight class and fueling. That is for a wrestler who is not in physical trouble today.
Support for that conversation may help later. He has not decided to move up, and his symptoms come first.
takeaway: When warning signs include acute physical symptoms, medical evaluation comes first and other referrals follow.

stem: In a first video interview, Hyun-seo, a professional esports player, is asked about the frustration ("tilt") that follows lost rounds. He says, "Am I stuck like this? No. I went a whole year on the academy roster without blowing up at anyone, and we lost plenty. That guy's still in here somewhere." The consultant reflects this back and notes it in the record. In motivational interviewing, what kind of change talk is it?
options: A statement of desire to change
A statement of reasons to change
A statement of ability to change
A statement of steps toward change
rationales: Desire talk tells what a person wants, as in "I wish" or "I'd like." Hyun-seo does not say what he wants.
Reason talk gives an argument for change, such as what tilt costs him. He gives no such argument.
Best. He answers "Am I stuck?" with proof from his own past that he can stay composed. That is ability talk, one of the preparatory forms of change talk.
Taking-steps talk reports recent action toward the change. His example is from a past season, offered as proof of what he can do.
takeaway: Past success offered as proof of what is possible is ability talk; taking steps is recent action.

stem: Wren, a masters cyclist, completed the ACSI-28 at intake and is curious about the results. "I hope you won't do what my old boss did with appraisals," she says. "He'd slide the sheet across, we'd go line by line, I'd nod, and on the train home I'd realize I hadn't taken in a word. Then I'd have a hundred questions." They meet again on Friday. What is the best way to give Wren her results?
options: Send her a plain summary to read before Friday
Go through each score with her on Friday
Open with her strengths on Friday, then the rest
Set the results aside and have her retake it Friday
rationales: Best. Her story shows that she takes things in on her own and comes up with questions later. Reading first lets her use Friday to ask them and to say how the results fit.
A line-by-line talk is a common way to give feedback, and it is the experience she says left her nodding and taking in nothing.
Strengths first can ease a client who is braced for bad news. Wren is curious and has a different problem with feedback.
Retesting makes sense when the answers may not be sound. Nothing suggests that hers are not.
takeaway: Feedback on results should suit the way the client takes in information.

stem: Marte, an elite sprint canoeist, used to lie awake before big regattas. Last season she filled out the CSAI-2 in the team hotel after dinner, on the eve of two national regattas, and her cognitive anxiety scores were high. She has since spent eight weeks practicing a wind-down routine. Two club regattas come up this month, and two national ones next month. Her coach is eager for news. When should the CSAI-2 be repeated to judge whether the routine is helping?
options: An hour before her races at the club regattas
An hour before her races at the national regattas
On the evening before the club regattas
On the evening before the national regattas
rationales: A club regatta and the final hour both differ from baseline. A lower score could come from the smaller stakes.
The stakes would match, but anxiety in the last hour may not resemble anxiety at bedtime, when her problem occurs.
The hour would match and the news would come sooner, but club events would likely stir less worry with or without a routine.
Best. State anxiety varies with the time to competition and with its importance. Matching both lets the new scores be compared with last season's.
takeaway: Repeat a state measure under the baseline conditions: the same kind of event at the same time before it.

stem: At intake, Nomvula, a collegiate tennis player, built a performance profile and rated herself on ten qualities. Ten weeks later she has met the targets she set, and her coach has moved her from singles to doubles for the rest of the year. Reading down the old sheet at their review, she laughs. "Patience from the baseline? I'm at the net all day now." She and the consultant want to use profiling to plan the next ten weeks. Which approach fits best?
options: Have her re-rate the ten qualities
Have her list new qualities and rate those
Have her coach rate her on the ten qualities
Have her rate how she now thinks she was at intake
rationales: Re-rating the same qualities is the usual way to review progress. She has met her targets, and the sheet no longer describes the game she plays.
Best. A profile's qualities belong to the performer's role as she sees it. Her role has changed, so planning calls for a new list even though it gives up comparison with the old one.
A coach's ratings help when the two see her differently. The trouble here is the list, not the rater.
A look back helps when the player's understanding of a quality has changed what her numbers mean. She plans to look ahead, and the qualities have lost their relevance.
takeaway: Re-rate a profile to measure progress; rebuild it when the role it describes has changed.

stem: Farah, an executive who meets with the consultant by video, has been learning paced breathing to settle herself before board presentations. Her log shows a session every night for six weeks. With her consent, the consultant sees wearable data showing that her breathing slows to the target pace within a minute. Her ratings of stress before presentations have not moved. "On board days I'm on the phone until the door opens," she says. Which reading best fits these results?
options: The skill is learned but is not used where it is needed
The skill is used where it is needed but does not suit her
The skill is helping in ways that her ratings do not show
The skill needs more practice before it can be judged
rationales: Best. She can slow her breathing quickly and practices nightly, yet a board day leaves her no moment to do it. The results show learning without transfer, so the technique has not been tested in presentations.
To conclude this, she would have to be using it before presentations. Her remark about the phone says that she is not.
Other signs of calmer presentations would be needed. There are none here, and she has not used it on those days.
More practice would be needed if she were slow to settle. Six weeks of nightly sessions and a one-minute response show that the skill is there.
takeaway: Before judging a technique, separate three questions: was it learned, was it used, and did it help?

stem: A consultant has run a team-building program for a collegiate rowing squad: shared dinners, a buddy system, and a service project. On the GEQ, given anonymously, the squad's social scores were low in September and are high in January, in all four boats. The captains have seen the change around the boathouse. "I'm convinced," says the coach. "But I have money and hours for one of the three this spring. Which do I keep?" What would best help the consultant answer?
options: Repeating the GEQ at the end of the season
Observing how rowers mix before and after practice
Holding focus groups with rowers from each boat
Comparing GEQ scores boat by boat
rationales: A later GEQ would show whether the gain lasts. It would come after the choice, and it gives no score for each activity.
Observation would check the scores against behavior. The coach accepts the change, and the captains have seen it.
Best. The GEQ shows that cohesion rose, not which activity brought it about. Rowers' accounts of the three activities speak to the coach's choice.
A breakdown by boat would show who gained. All four did, and they shared the same three activities.
takeaway: Outcome scores show whether a program worked; to learn which part helped, ask the participants.

stem: Teodor, a professional alpine skier, began working with a consultant in summer and has completed the TOPS three times. From fall to midwinter, his practice scores for self-talk stayed high. In competition, his self-talk score fell by a third and his automaticity score rose by about as much, with other scores steady. He has had his best four results of the season. "I used to talk myself down the whole hill," he says. "Now I just ski." Which next step do these data best support?
options: Adding race simulations so that self-talk carries over
Reteaching the self-talk cues that have slipped
Asking what has been unsettling him on race days
Continuing as they are through the rest of the season
rationales: Simulations help skills move from training to races. His race self-talk was in place and has given way to something that is working.
Reteaching would suit a lost skill. His practice scores show that he still has it.
Race-day trouble would show in other scores, such as emotional control or negative thinking, or in results. Those are steady or better.

Best. Less deliberate self-talk with more automaticity and better results looks like a skill that no longer needs effort. Nothing calls for a change, and asking for more self-talk could get in his way.
takeaway: A drop in deliberate strategy use can mean progress; read it beside automaticity and results.

stem: Leopold, a firefighter, is working on recovering his composure in the minutes after a serious alarm. Some weeks bring six such calls and some bring none. In the first month the consultant asked each Sunday how the week had gone. "Fine, I think," he said, or, "There was a bad one, or was that the week before?" On the drive back to the station, though, he can describe a call to the minute. Which way of tracking his progress fits best?
options: A five-item rating that he completes on Sunday evenings
A two-item rating that he completes after serious calls
A checklist that his officer completes after each shift
A full skills inventory that he completes each month
rationales: Weekly ratings suit a state that builds or fades over days. His problem is tied to calls, and by Sunday he has lost the details.
Best. The target occurs in single events that come irregularly, and he remembers them well just afterward. Event-based ratings catch each one while it is fresh.
An officer's view helps with signs the client misses. Leopold can describe his own calls well, if asked soon enough.
A full inventory shows broad change in mental skills. It would not show what happens after particular alarms.
takeaway: Match the timing of measurement to the target: irregular events call for ratings tied to the event.

stem: With his consent, a consultant at a national training center has given Yerlan, an elite long-track speed skater, the POMS every week since spring. Ten days into a heavy block, his fatigue is up and his vigor down, as happened in last year's block, and both ease after rest days. His tension and anger scores have doubled as well. Looking back over the chart, the consultant sees that those two began to climb during his week of leave, before the block. What should the consultant do next?
options: Ask him what has been happening away from training
Talk over with him how the training block is going
Plan with him what to tell his coach about recovery
Help him set up a visit with a licensed clinician
rationales: Best. Fatigue and vigor follow the load, but tension and anger rose while he was resting. Training cannot explain a change that came before it, so the consultant should find out what else is going on.
A talk about the block suits mood changes that follow the load. Fatigue and vigor do, and they ease with rest; the two scores that stand out began to climb before it.
This suits fatigue and vigor that stay poor with rest. His recover after rest days.
Referral fits signs of a mental health concern, such as lasting low mood or loss of interest. Two raised scores with no known reason call for a talk first.
takeaway: Line up mood scores with the training calendar; a change that comes before the load has another source.

stem: Before teaching Saoirse, a collegiate diver, a pre-dive routine, the consultant coded video of three meets, timing her from the referee's whistle to takeoff. Six weeks into the routine, an intern coded three more meets, timing her from her first step along the board. The second set of times averages four seconds shorter and varies little from dive to dive. The coach is delighted that she has "stopped dawdling." What should the consultant do before drawing a conclusion?
options: Have three more meets timed from the first step
Have her note after each dive which steps she completed
Have the later meets timed again from the whistle
Have practice dives timed from the first step
rationales: More meets help when results are few or scattered. These are consistent, and more of them timed from the first step would leave the problem in place.
Self-report adds what a camera cannot see. The conclusion in question is about time, which video can show.
Best. The two sets start the clock at different points, so the four seconds may come from the rule and not from Saoirse. Applying the baseline definition makes the sets comparable.
Practice video would test use in another setting. It cannot tell whether her meet times changed.
takeaway: Before comparing observations, confirm that both sets use the same behavioral definition.
